analysis.one_liner: Creates a national health insurance program covering doctor, hospital, dental and nursing care, funded by a new value-added tax.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in House committees from early 2001 until the Congress ended in January 2003, with just one cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would set up a national health insurance program run through states and local boards, giving every worker who qualifies (based on Social Security wage records) coverage for medical, hospital, dental, podiatric, home-nursing and lab services, with free choice of doctor and hospital. It would be paid for by a new national sales-style tax (a value-added tax) with zero rates on food, housing, and medical care, deposited in a dedicated trust fund. The bill was introduced by Rep. John Dingell and referred to two House committees, which took no further action beyond a subcommittee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Working people and their dependents who qualify under the wage-record rules would get coverage without premiums or deductibles for doctor visits, hospital stays, dental and nursing care. People unable to meet the shattering cost of serious illness, and families currently priced out of preventive care, would benefit most.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Uninsured and underinsured workers and families

how_it_helps.text: Every eligible individual may freely choose their physician, dentist, podiatrist, nurse, or hospital, and may change that choice; hospital services, medical, dental and home-nursing care are provided as benefits without deductibles or coinsurance described in the bill.

Eligibility is tied to wage records used for Social Security, so steady low- and middle-wage workers and Social Security beneficiaries qualify, and states can buy the same services for needy uninsured people using existing federal grant funds.

The bill would replace payment for care based on unpredictable out-of-pocket costs with a prepaid social-insurance model, which its findings section says the voluntary insurance system cannot achieve.
Payments to hospitals are based on reasonable cost with possible maximum rates, and the bill prohibits discrimination by race, creed, or color in providing services.

analysis.who_pays: The program is funded by a new value-added tax on commercial transactions, collected by sellers; consumers bear it through prices, though food, housing, and medical care are taxed at zero. Private health insurers and the existing employer-based insurance system would lose their central role, since the new program is the payer for covered care.
analysis.who_pays_short: Consumers via a new VAT; private insurers

drawbacks.text: The value-added tax is a consumption tax, which generally falls more heavily on lower-income households than a progressive income tax, even with the bill's zero rates on food, housing, and medical care.

Coverage is limited: hospital care is capped at 60 days per year, hospitalization in mental-disease institutions is excluded (with a 30-day limit after a psychosis diagnosis), and the Board may limit dental, home-nursing, and auxiliary services when personnel, facilities, or funds are inadequate.
Eligibility depends on a wage-record history; people with weak work records are covered only if a public agency reimburses the fund, which could leave gaps for the poorest individuals.
The bill does not clearly phase out Medicare; people entitled to Medicare can get new benefits only for services Medicare does not cover, with a study of a later merger.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people without dependable coverage, the upside is large: no premiums or deductibles and free choice of provider. The costs are real too — a new national consumption tax, tighter benefit limits than critics of government programs usually acknowledge (60 hospital days, possible service rationing where funds run short), and a genuine administrative transition from today's mixed system. The bill is also unusually thin on how the VAT rate would be set and how a large transition would be managed, so even a supporter should call it a starting framework rather than a finished program.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees on the day it was introduced, passed along to a Health subcommittee a month later, and nothing more ever happened before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John D. Dingell introduced the National Health Insurance Act in the House on January 3, 2001.
The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, and on February 7, 2001 it was referred to the Health subcommittee.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote is recorded; the bill died when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.
The bill had a single cosponsor, one House Democrat, over its two-year life.
The bill would have funded coverage through a new value-added tax flowing into a National Health Care Trust Fund.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers and the employer-based insurance status quo, which were never displaced; households also avoided the new consumption tax the bill would have imposed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private insurers and the coverage status quo

for.name: Rep. John D. Dingell
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the National Health Insurance Act on the first day of the 107th Congress.

for.name: 1 of 208 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no other members joined over its two-year life.

against.name: Committee leadership, House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means
against.role: Chairs of the committees of referral (Republican-controlled committees in this Congress)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it sat referred to committee and then subcommittee for two years.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes on the bill; its only support came from two House Democrats, and the Republican-run committees of referral took no action on it.

industries.note: The program would become the payer for covered care, ending the private-insurance role for medical, dental, and hospital coverage (voluntary plans could only act as agents or providers). Keeping the status quo is what allowed insurers to keep collecting premiums; ordinary people without coverage paid the price of that outcome.
Hospitals would gain guaranteed payment at reasonable cost for all eligible patients, but payment could be capped and is based on the least expensive accommodations available.

Every eligible patient becomes a potential payer through the program, but compensation is set by fee schedules or per-capita and salary methods, and the bill requires rates to reflect local conditions and professional incomes.
Employers would no longer be expected to finance health benefits, but the value-added tax would add a new compliance burden and reach consumer prices.

industries.industry: Pharmaceutical makers and suppliers of medical goods
industries.note: Coverage includes unusually expensive prescribed drugs, appliances, and eyeglasses as auxiliary services, but the Board can limit or restrict these when funds are inadequate.
